title: Topic 9 Economic change - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Table 9.13 shows changes in South Korea's economy between 1970 and 2022. Define the term: Secondary industries.

points: Manufacturing and processing industries that change raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for definition of secondary industries as manufacturing/processing.

points: Industries that provide commercial, personal, and professional services to people and businesses (e.g. retail, finance, education, health) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for definition of tertiary industries as service-providing.

questions.question_text: Describe the changes in South Korea's employment structure between 1970 and 2022 as shown in Table 9.13.

points: Primary industries saw a dramatic decline of almost 90%, falling from 50.4% in 1970 to only 5.4% in 2022 [1]
Secondary industries increased from 14.3% in 1970 to 24.5% in 2022 (an increase of over 70%) [1]
Tertiary industries doubled, surging from 35.3% in 1970 to 70.1% in 2022, becoming the dominant sector [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for describing trends in primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors with figures.

questions.question_text: Suggest reasons for the change in employment structure in South Korea between 1970 and 2022.

points: Agricultural mechanisation and modern technology reduced the need for farm labour, pushing workers off the land [1]
Government industrial policy and foreign investment heavily promoted export-oriented manufacturing (e.g. ship building, automobiles, electronics like Samsung/Hyundai) [1]
Rising household incomes and living standards created huge consumer demand for domestic services (retailing, leisure, finance, personal services) [1]
Higher levels of education and technology produced a skilled workforce suited for high-end tertiary and quaternary service sectors [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for explaining mechanisation of farming, industrial growth, and expansion of service economy.

points: The increasing interconnectedness and interdependence of the world through economic, cultural, technological, and political links [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for definition of globalisation as increasing interconnectedness/interdependence.

points: TNCs establish global supply chains, offshoring manufacturing to LICs/MICs while keeping R&D and headquarters in HICs [1]
They drive Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), transferring capital, modern technology, and management practices worldwide [1]
They spread global brands, consumer goods, and Western culture (e.g. McDonald's, Apple, Nike) across continents [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for explaining supply chains, FDI/technology transfer, and global branding.

questions.question_text: Assess the impact of globalisation at a local scale.

points: Positive impacts: Influx of foreign investment and employment creation with higher wages; wider consumer choice of imported goods and cuisines; improved local transport infrastructure [1-2]

Negative impacts: Local small businesses and domestic craftsmen fail to compete against multinational corporations; sudden closure or relocation of TNC factories creates massive local unemployment; erosion of local cultural heritage and traditions [1-2]
Social impacts: Increased cultural diversity through migration, but potential social friction or brain drain of skilled local youth [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 5 marks for balanced assessment of positive and negative local impacts.

questions.question_text: Using named examples, evaluate the impacts of TNCs on host countries.

inputs.label: Nhập bài làm Case Study (7 marks):

points: Positive impacts: Creation of direct and indirect employment (multiplier effect); capital inflow and government tax revenues; technology transfer and workforce training; export earnings boosting GDP [2-3 marks]

Negative impacts: Profit repatriation where profits flow back to HIC headquarters rather than host economy; exploitation of cheap labour with poor working conditions / sweatshops; environmental pollution and resource depletion (e.g. oil spills); overdependence on a foreign firm that may leave for cheaper locations [2-3 marks]
Named examples: e.g. Nike / Samsung in Vietnam, Shell in Nigeria, Foxconn / Apple in China [1-2 marks]
Evaluation: Weighing economic development against social and environmental costs, noting that effective host government regulation is critical to maximizing benefits [1 mark]
marking_scheme.rubric: Level 1 (1-3 marks): Simple points about multinational companies without balance or named examples. Level 2 (4-6 marks): Explains both benefits (jobs, capital) and drawbacks (sweatshops, environmental damage, profit leakage) with named example. Level 3 (7 marks): Comprehensive evaluation assessing net impact on host country, supported by specific named case study details, concluding with a nuanced judgement.
